title: Ambrose reading silently (6.3)
hook: Augustine is struck that Ambrose reads without moving his lips
tomorrow: can you keep your eyes shut when a whole arena roars?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Milan, and a bishop who received Augustine like a father before any argument. The line: the bishop received me.

Three group chats, an inbox, a parent's opinion at dinner, a coach's voicemail. Some weeks are all voices, and your own is the hardest to hear. Augustine had a week like that, full of questions, and walked into the bishop's house to ask them. The door stood open to anyone. And what was Ambrose doing that Augustine couldn't stop watching? Reading. His eyes moved down the page. His lips didn't.
screen: `A WEEK OF VOICES.` → `THE DOOR STOOD OPEN.` → `EYES MOVING, LIPS STILL.`

segments.voice: Augustine describes it carefully. When Ambrose read, his eyes ran over the pages and his heart searched out the sense, but his voice and tongue were at rest. Nobody announced visitors in that house, so people would sit in silence a long while, then leave, not wanting to interrupt someone so absorbed. Augustine wonders why he read that way. Maybe Ambrose didn't want a listener stopping him at a hard passage and using up his little free time. Maybe he was saving a voice that easily grew hoarse. Whatever the reason, Augustine says, in such a man it was a good one. And Augustine's own questions had to wait. The bishop's hours went to crowds of people with their troubles, and the few moments left he spent feeding his body or his mind. So what does this give a person in a loud week? A picture worth keeping: eyes on one page, the heart looking for the sense, the voice at rest. And a surprise. Augustine got his answers without the private talk he wanted. On Sundays he heard Ambrose explain the scriptures to everyone, and began to see the Church's teaching wasn't what he'd assumed.
screen: `EYES READ, THE HEART SEARCHES.` · `VOICE AND TONGUE AT REST.` · `HIS QUESTIONS HAD TO WAIT.` · `ANSWERS CAME ON SUNDAYS.` · then, large: `READING IN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Open a short passage you have nearby, a psalm or a few lines of any book you trust. Read it with your eyes only, slowly, lips at rest, and let your heart look for the sense. When you reach the end, stay there in the quiet.
Ambrose reading silently. Eyes on the page, heart searching the sense, voice and tongue at rest: the scene that held Augustine at the bishop's door.
Here's your line: reading in silence, where the eyes read and the heart looks for the sense. Until next time.

screen: `DAY 1440 COUNTS.` → `THE CONFESSIONS, READ THROUGH · 14 OF 35.` → `TOMORROW: CAN YOU KEEP YOUR EYES SHUT WHEN A WHOLE ARENA ROARS?`

howItsDone: Catholics practice slow, prayerful reading of scripture, often called lectio divina: reading a short passage quietly, more than once, and letting it sink in. Some keep a few minutes of silent reading each day.

Ambrose.meaning: the bishop of Milan, honored as a saint

Augustine.meaning: a North African bishop who wrote the Confessions as a prayer

scriptures.meaning: the holy writings of the Bible

notes: Confessions 6.3 paraphrased: when Ambrose read, his eyes ran over the pages and his heart searched out the sense, but voice and tongue were at rest; no one was forbidden to enter nor announced; visitors sat long in silence and departed; Augustine's guesses (avoiding questions on obscure passages, preserving a voice easily made hoarse); 'with what intent soever he did it, certainly in such a man it was good'; crowds of busy people; each Lord's day Augustine heard him rightly expounding scripture. Confirm.
